items.title: DNA-editing ‘pencils’ probe early human development
items.summary: A genome-rewriting approach known as adenine base editing offers a precise way to investigate gene function in early human embryos.

items.title: Imaging cellular activity across all organs reveals body-wide circuits
items.summary: An imaging system developed to record cellular activity throughout the whole body of zebrafish captures cellular organ dynamics and identifies multiple distributed circuits.

items.title: AI model predicts which breast-cancer drugs work best
items.summary: Model trained on millions of protein measurements can gauge drug effectiveness in tissue samples taken from people with triple-negative breast cancer.

items.title: Highly efficient base editing at PCSK9 and normal human embryo development
items.summary: Highly efficient base editing at PCSK9 and normal human embryo development

items.title: Breaking timescales with generative sampling of conformational transitions
items.summary: A generative committor-guided path-sampling framework reconstructs rare biomolecular transition pathways and reveals the underlying thermodynamics and kinetics without using predefined collective variables or brute-force sampling, at an acceptable computational cost.

items.title: Bacteria recruited to treat cancer
items.summary: Anticancer drugs could be manufactured and delivered by modified microorganisms.

items.title: Neocortical long-range inhibition promotes cortical synchrony and sleep
items.summary: In mice, a sparse population of sleep-active long-range inhibitory neurons in the neocortex promote widespread cortical synchronization and sleep, revealing a cortical mechanism that contributes to the regulation of sleep.

items.title: Predicting genome-wide functional constraints with GPN-Star
items.summary: GPN-Star, a genomic language model with a phylogeny-aware architecture for whole-genome alignment data, is shown to be a scalable and flexible tool for genetic variant effect prediction across species.

items.title: Drug-delivering particles aim to breach the blood–brain barrier
items.summary: The inability to get drugs into the brain has impeded the treatment of cancer and neurodegenerative diseases for decades. Techniques based on nanoparticles and exosomes are vying to provide a solution.

items.title: Proximity-guided graph learning reveals tumour-associated proximity antigens
items.summary: A proximity-mapping atlas defines tumour-associated proximity antigens, revealing disease-associated membrane spatial communities, and identifies EGFR–CDCP1 as a co-target pair that enhances tumour killing by multispecific therapeutics.

items.title: An operational perturbation proteomics-based virtual cell model
items.summary: Temporal protein-abundance measurements from systematically perturbed breast cancer cell lines were generated to develop ProteinTalks, a virtual cell model that functions as an operational tool for diverse drug discovery tasks.

items.title: A serpin–myeloid axis in pancreatic cancer heterogeneity and immune evasion
items.summary: SERPINE1 and SERPINB2-driven fibrin-rich niches locally programme immunosuppressive macrophages and exclude T cells, enabling spatially organized immune evasion in pancreatic ductal carcinoma.

items.title: TRI-611, a selective, brain-penetrant molecular glue degrader of ALK
items.summary: TRI-611 induces the degradation of ALK fusion proteins via a previously undescribed CRBN recruitment motif, and its preclinical anti-tumour activity highlights TRI-611 as a potential new way of treating ALK-positive non-small-cell lung cancer.

items.title: Special delivery: bacterial couriers are smuggling drugs into cancers
items.summary: Microorganisms that deliver treatments to tumours could make chemotherapy, radiotherapy and immunotherapy safer and more effective.

items.title: Uniform film formation helps tandem solar cells work better for longer
items.summary: When making mixed-halide perovskite films for use in solar cells, bromide-rich domains crystallize faster than iodide-rich ones do, leading to defects. Adding a molecule tuned to bind selectively to bromide-bound lead synchronizes the crystallization rates, yielding uniform films, better operating stability and a more-efficient perovskite–organic tandem.

items.title: The neurons that can put a brake on a nervous-system cancer
items.summary: Drugs that imitate the effect of GABAergic neurons slow the growth of tumours called gliomas in mice.

items.title: PLA2G2D in tumour-draining lymph nodes regulates anti-tumour immunity
authors: Thierry P. P. van den Bosch
items.summary: A specific population of macrophages that express high levels of the enzyme PLA2G2D in tumour-draining lymph nodes is associated with poor prognosis in patients, and inhibiting PLA2G2D improves anti-tumour immunity in mouse models.

items.title: These six advances could change how drugs are delivered
items.summary: Medication triggered by your circadian clock, self-assembling delivery systems based on DNA and other highlights from studies and trials.

items.title: Ancient proteins identify various Denisovan remains from Southwest China
items.summary: Identification and proteomic analysis of bone fragments and teeth from an excavation in Southwest China provide insight into the evolution and phenotype of Denisovans and fill a geographical gap in their documented distribution.

items.title: Anodic Pd membrane H<sub>2</sub> extraction enhances thermochemical dehydrogenation
items.summary: An electrochemical cell with molten hydroxide and a Pd membrane actively extracts H2 and thereby boosts ammonia and methylcyclohexane conversion, while also delivering purified H2 ready for use.

items.title: Integrated signatures define mutational processes in prostate cancer
items.summary: Eight integrated mutational footprints collectively explain the mutational processes in 85% of primary prostate cancer genomes.

items.title: Who were the Denisovans? Rich trove of fossils and tools paints new picture
items.summary: Objects found in a cave in southwestern China suggest that these enigmatic ancient humans were accomplished hunters.

items.title: Within-family effect of ancestry on complex traits in a Mexican population
items.summary: This study uses a within-family design to identify significant ancestry differences in complex traits such as height and type 2 diabetes in a genetically diverse population from Mexico City.

items.title: Foaming photopolymers as a high-resolution biomimetic printing platform
items.summary: Deep-foam photolithography uses light-controlled polymer foaming to create high-resolution, multifunctional microstructures with tunable optical, wetting and fluid-handling properties for advanced manufacturing applications.

items.title: TM184C is a GPCR-like regulator of intercellular exchange and autophagy
items.summary: TM184C—an ancient G-protein-coupled receptor-like superdark protein involved in regulation of autophagy, intercellular connectivity and material exchange—underscores the promise of exploring the understudied human proteome and beyond.

items.title: Daily briefing: OpenAI claims a huge maths breakthrough
items.summary: The AI giant claims to have solved one of maths’ trickiest problems, but questions swirl over should get the credit. Plus, an atlas of every single DNA letter mutation in humans and why more bioengineered microorganisms aren’t making it out of the lab.

items.title: Denisovans from southwestern China and their subsistence strategies
items.summary: Evidence from Bianfu Cave shows specialized hunting, expedient stone-tool production and extensive bone use of Denisovans, providing new insights into their ecology, behaviour and cultural legacy in eastern Asia.

items.title: Distant sensors announced a fearsome tsunami’s birth
items.summary: Seismic data pinpoint the collapse of an underwater volcano, and reveal how the eruption triggered a destructive tsunami.

items.title: Advancing conflict research and response through satellite-derived data
items.summary: Integrating satellite-derived war-damage data with text-based fatality records through improvement, enrichment and fusion mitigates limitations inherent in each source, revealing complex violence dynamics beyond fatality-centric paradigms, as case studies from Ukraine and Myanmar illustrate.

items.title: Combined satellite and news data capture unseen aspects of war
items.summary: Records of war extracted from news reports have shaped what researchers know about violence. Satellite images could transform that understanding — if access stays open.

items.title: Mobile education builds resilience during shocks in five countries
items.summary: Remote phone-based targeted tutoring in five countries produced large, cost-effective learning gains during school closures, outperforming text messaging and working effectively when delivered by governments or non-governmental organizations to strengthen education resilience.

items.title: Phone-call tutorials improve learning cost-effectively during education emergencies
items.summary: Across five randomized trials in India, Kenya, Nepal, the Philippines and Uganda, weekly 20-minute mobile-phone-call tutorials produced large learning gains for primary-school children during school closures caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Governments can keep children learning through societal shocks using this approach, which combines low-cost, high-access mobile-phone technology with high-quality tutoring targeted to each child’s learning level.

items.title: Rivers deliver unexpectedly high loads of microplastics to the sea
items.summary: Intense rains coupled with poor waste management cause big spikes in pollution.

items.title: Phone tutoring boosts math scores when schools are forced to close
items.summary: Evidence suggests that regular calls can keep kids learning when schooling is disrupted — plus, why a familiar world map may be about to change.

items.title: Popular open-science platform to stop hosting data and code amid funding concerns
items.summary: Changes to the Open Science Framework’s policies will come into effect in November, forcing researchers to reconsider their workflows.

items.title: Phone-based tutoring improves learning during school closures
items.summary: One-to-one phone sessions substantially increased students’ numeracy test scores in low- and middle-income countries that experience emergencies that disrupt schooling.

items.title: Pick up the phone! Phone calls with tutors keep kids learning when schools shut down
items.summary: The low-cost intervention was trialled in five countries during the COVID-19 pandemic.

items.title: A good drug is useless if it misses its target
items.summary: The best medicines go exactly where they’re needed in the body— and nowhere else.

items.title: El Niño goes viral — and scientists learn what makes people care about the climate
items.summary: Evoking emotions is more likely to prompt people to engage with climate efforts than is data alone.

items.title: Ruins of ancient Asian city show engineering prowess and organization
items.summary: The 5,000-year-old city of Liangzhu has mounds, dams and city walls built in a challenging waterlogged site.

items.title: Medicines do no good if people don’t take them
items.summary: Health psychologist Rob Horne explains why medication non-adherence is such a problem, and how behavioural science can help to address it.

items.title: Use AI as a sparring partner, not an oracle
items.summary: As artificial-intelligence tools become crucial collaborators in science, universities must teach students to challenge such systems and assess their ability to do so.

items.title: Hello Equal Earth: what the UN’s new world map will change
items.summary: What the UN vote to ditch the Mercator projection means for education, navigation and public perception.

items.title: AI researchers reckon with the $1.5 million ‘academia tax’
items.summary: Academics explain that their research freedom beats the increased salary they would get in the corporate sector, but emerging hybrid models might allow them to get the best of both worlds.

items.title: Why we need an International Panel on Inequality
items.summary: Disparities in income and wealth are growing. A scientific assessment process can give governments the information they need to tackle them.

items.title: Successful early-career scientists rely on network of mentors
items.summary: Large networks are particularly beneficial to researchers in under-represented groups.

items.title: Why the super-fun Ig Nobel prizes bring serious value to science
items.summary: Awards that celebrate humour, curiosity and irreverence are a balm in hard times.

items.title: How AI is changing PhD programmes: join our free webinar
items.summary: Learn how artificial intelligence can hone your research skills as well as the potential pitfalls of relying too heavily on it.

items.title: In the basement of miniaturized relics
items.summary: Thinking small.

items.title: Author Correction: The molecular basis of force selectivity by PIEZO2
items.summary: Author Correction: The molecular basis of force selectivity by PIEZO2
